claim: Unresolved ER stress followed by cell death is recognized as the main cause of neonatal diabetes.
source: Unresolved ER stress followed by cell death is recognized as the main cause of a multitude of pathologies including neonatal diabetes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: A mutation in the proinsulin gene causes a severe form of permanent neonatal diabetes in Akita mice.
source: A systematic analysis of the mechanisms of β-cell loss and dysfunction in Akita mice, in which a mutation in the proinsulin gene causes a severe form of permanent neonatal diabetes
evidence: This is a known characteristic of the Akita mouse model.

claim: There is no increase in β-cell apoptosis throughout life in Akita mice.
source: A systematic analysis of the mechanisms of β-cell loss and dysfunction in Akita mice, in which a mutation in the proinsulin gene causes a severe form of permanent neonatal diabetes, showed no increase in β-cell apoptosis throughout life.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the systematic analysis conducted in the study.

claim: The main mechanism leading to β-cell dysfunction in Akita mice is marked impairment of β-cell growth during early postnatal life.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the main mechanism leading to β-cell dysfunction is marked impairment of β-cell growth during the early postnatal life due to transient inhibition of mTORC1, which governs postnatal β-cell growth and differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis.

claim: Impaired β-cell growth in Akita mice is due to transient inhibition of mTORC1.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the main mechanism leading to β-cell dysfunction is marked impairment of β-cell growth during the early postnatal life due to transient inhibition of mTORC1, which governs postnatal β-cell growth and differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis.

claim: mTORC1 governs postnatal β-cell growth and differentiation.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the main mechanism leading to β-cell dysfunction is marked impairment of β-cell growth during the early postnatal life due to transient inhibition of mTORC1, which governs postnatal β-cell growth and differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Restoration of mTORC1 activity in neonate β-cells is sufficient to rescue postnatal β-cell growth in Akita mice.
source: Importantly, restoration of mTORC1 activity in neonate β-cells was sufficient to rescue postnatal β-cell growth, and to improve diabetes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Restoration of mTORC1 activity in neonate β-cells improves diabetes in Akita mice.
source: Importantly, restoration of mTORC1 activity in neonate β-cells was sufficient to rescue postnatal β-cell growth, and to improve diabetes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Early-life events inducing ER stress affect β-cell mass expansion due to mTOR inhibition in permanent neonatal diabetes.
source: We propose a scenario for the development of permanent neonatal diabetes, possibly also common forms of diabetes, where early-life events inducing ER stress affect β-cell mass expansion due to mTOR inhibition.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: Early-life events inducing ER stress may affect β-cell mass expansion in common forms of diabetes.
source: We propose a scenario for the development of permanent neonatal diabetes, possibly also common forms of diabetes, where early-life events inducing ER stress affect β-cell mass expansion due to mTOR inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the study's findings to common diabetes forms.

claim: β-Cell failure is the fundamental pathophysiological factor of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
source: β-Cell failure is the fundamental pathophysiological factor of both type 1 (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) (Cerasi and Luft, 1967; Accili et al., 2010; Rhodes, 2005; Mathis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Proinsulin mutations lead to proinsulin misfolding, inducing β-cell ER stress and permanent neonatal diabetes.
source: An example is proinsulin mutations which lead to proinsulin misfolding, inducing β-cell ER stress and consequently permanent neonatal diabetes, also called mutant-insulin diabetes of the young (MIDY); its animal counterpart is the Akita mouse (Liu et al., 2010; Weiss, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: β-Cells have a highly developed endoplasmic reticulum to cope with the demand to secrete high amounts of insulin.
source: β-Cells have a highly developed endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to cope with the demand to secrete high amounts of insulin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-cell biology.

claim: In diabetes, the proinsulin burden on the ER is increased and proinsulin folding is impaired due to altered β-cell redox state.
source: In diabetes, the proinsulin burden on the ER is increased and proinsulin folding is impaired due to altered β-cell redox state, hence leading to accumulation of misfolded proinsulin and consequently to ER stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge about diabetes pathophysiology.

claim: Proinsulin misfolding/ER stress plays an important role in the pathophysiology of T1D and T2D.
source: Therefore, proinsulin misfolding/ER stress also plays an important role in the pathophysiology of T1D and T2D (Eizirik et al., 2008; Scheuner and Kaufman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: β-Cell mass is reduced in diabetes.
source: β-Cell mass is reduced in diabetes (Rahier et al., 2008; Butler et al., 2003), albeit with very large variation between subjects, even in T1D (Campbell-Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is very large variation in β-cell mass between subjects with diabetes, even in T1D.
source: β-Cell mass is reduced in diabetes (Rahier et al., 2008; Butler et al., 2003), albeit with very large variation between subjects, even in T1D (Campbell-Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Impaired programming of the endocrine pancreas in utero is implicated in β-cell mass reduction in diabetes.
source: Several mechanisms are implicated, including impaired programming of the endocrine pancreas in utero (Sandovici et al., 2013; Alejandro et al., 2014), increased β-cell apoptosis (Butler et al., 2003; Jurgens et al., 2011; Donath et al., 1999), reduced β-cell proliferation (Butler et al., 2007), and dedifferentiation of mature β-cells (Talchai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased β-cell apoptosis is implicated in β-cell mass reduction in diabetes.
source: Several mechanisms are implicated, including impaired programming of the endocrine pancreas in utero (Sandovici et al., 2013; Alejandro et al., 2014), increased β-cell apoptosis (Butler et al., 2003; Jurgens et al., 2011; Donath et al., 1999), reduced β-cell proliferation (Butler et al., 2007), and dedifferentiation of mature β-cells (Talchai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Reduced β-cell proliferation is implicated in β-cell mass reduction in diabetes.
source: Several mechanisms are implicated, including impaired programming of the endocrine pancreas in utero (Sandovici et al., 2013; Alejandro et al., 2014), increased β-cell apoptosis (Butler et al., 2003; Jurgens et al., 2011; Donath et al., 1999), reduced β-cell proliferation (Butler et al., 2007), and dedifferentiation of mature β-cells (Talchai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dedifferentiation of mature β-cells is implicated in β-cell mass reduction in diabetes.
source: Several mechanisms are implicated, including impaired programming of the endocrine pancreas in utero (Sandovici et al., 2013; Alejandro et al., 2014), increased β-cell apoptosis (Butler et al., 2003; Jurgens et al., 2011; Donath et al., 1999), reduced β-cell proliferation (Butler et al., 2007), and dedifferentiation of mature β-cells (Talchai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: β-Cell mass expands rapidly in the newborn and then adjusts to changes in metabolic demand, probably also in humans.
source: β-Cell mass expands rapidly in the newborn and then adjusts to changes in metabolic demand, probably also in humans (Bonner-Weir et al., 2016; Cigliola et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research, with speculation about humans.

claim: In mice, islet and β-cell numbers are increased more than 3-fold between 10 days of age and adulthood.
source: In mice, islet and β-cell numbers are increased more than 3-fold between 10 days of age and adulthood; this is associated with high β-cell replication, which is drastically decreased during adulthood (Herbach et al., 2011; Teta et al., 2005; Saisho et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The increase in β-cell numbers in mice is associated with high β-cell replication, which is drastically decreased during adulthood.
source: In mice, islet and β-cell numbers are increased more than 3-fold between 10 days of age and adulthood; this is associated with high β-cell replication, which is drastically decreased during adulthood (Herbach et al., 2011; Teta et al., 2005; Saisho et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: β-Cell mass expansion is mainly mediated via proliferation of mature β-cells.
source: β-Cell mass expansion is mainly mediated via proliferation of mature β-cells (Dor et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Insulin demand drives β-cell proliferation via the unfolded protein response (UPR).
source: It has been recently suggested that insulin demand drives β-cell proliferation via the unfolded protein response (UPR), which senses insulin production.
evidence: This is a recent suggestion from the literature.

claim: UPR activation during ER stress correlated with and triggered β-cell proliferation in response to glucose, probably through ATF6.
source: UPR activation during ER stress correlated with and triggered β-cell proliferation in response to glucose, probably through ATF6 (24).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Reducing the proinsulin load by deleting the insulin gene decreased UPR along with increased β-cell proliferation.
source: Others showed that reducing the proinsulin load by deleting the insulin gene decreased UPR along with increased β-cell proliferation (Szabat et al., 2016), suggesting that ER stress is implicated in the regulation of β-cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ER stress is implicated in the regulation of β-cell proliferation.
source: Others showed that reducing the proinsulin load by deleting the insulin gene decreased UPR along with increased β-cell proliferation (Szabat et al., 2016), suggesting that ER stress is implicated in the regulation of β-cell proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference from cited research.

claim: Exposure to ER stress during the neonatal period dramatically reduces β-cell growth and functional maturation in Akita mice.
source: We found that exposure to ER stress during the neonatal period dramatically reduces β-cell growth and functional maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: Impairment of early β-cell growth and maturation leads to permanent β-cell dysfunction with subsequent development of diabetes in Akita mice.
source: Impairment of early β-cell growth and maturation leads to permanent β-cell dysfunction with subsequent development of diabetes; restoration of mTORC1 activity in Akita neonates was sufficient to prevent β-cell loss and ameliorate diabetes.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: Restoration of mTORC1 activity in Akita neonates is sufficient to prevent β-cell loss and ameliorate diabetes.
source: Impairment of early β-cell growth and maturation leads to permanent β-cell dysfunction with subsequent development of diabetes; restoration of mTORC1 activity in Akita neonates was sufficient to prevent β-cell loss and ameliorate diabetes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: Adult Akita mice develop severe insulin-deficient diabetes with fed blood glucose ~ 400 mg/dl.
source: Adult Akita mice develop severe insulin-deficient diabetes with fed blood glucose ~ 400 mg/dl along with a 90% decrease of pancreatic insulin content (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: Adult Akita mice have a 90% decrease of pancreatic insulin content.
source: Adult Akita mice develop severe insulin-deficient diabetes with fed blood glucose ~ 400 mg/dl along with a 90% decrease of pancreatic insulin content (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c.

claim: β-cell mass was decreased by 70% in adult Akita mice compared to age-matched controls.
source: In adult Akita mice, β-cell mass was decreased by 70% compared to age-matched controls (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The rate of β-cell proliferation measured by Ki67 staining was < 1% and similar in control and Akita mice.
source: The rate of β-cell proliferation measured by Ki67 staining was < 1% and similar in control and Akita mice (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: There was a slight increase in the number of TUNEL+ β-cells in adult Akita mice.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Izumi et al., 2003), there was a slight increase in the number of TUNEL+ β-cells in Akita mice (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b and a citation to prior research.

claim: Most islets in adult Akita mice contained no or only a single TUNEL+ β-cell.
source: Most islets contained no or only a single TUNEL+ β-cell.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data.

claim: The frequency of TUNEL+ cells was 0.1% in adult Akita mice, whereas no TUNEL+ cells were observed in control mice.
source: We counted 2592 β-cells in wild type and 1754 cells in Akita mice and found that the frequency of TUNEL+ cells was 0.1% in Akita mice, whereas no TUNEL+ cells were observed in control mice; the difference between groups was not statistically significant (p=0.1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data.

claim: The difference in TUNEL+ cell frequency between adult Akita and control mice was not statistically significant.
source: We counted 2592 β-cells in wild type and 1754 cells in Akita mice and found that the frequency of TUNEL+ cells was 0.1% in Akita mice, whereas no TUNEL+ cells were observed in control mice; the difference between groups was not statistically significant (p=0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study's data.

claim: The frequency of apoptotic events based on TUNEL was fairly low in adult Akita β-cells.
source: Thus, the frequency of apoptotic events based on TUNEL was fairly low in Akita β-cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's data.

claim: In adult Akita mice, the number of genetically labeled β-cells that stained negative for insulin increased by 2.6-fold compared with wild-type mice.
source: In Akita mice, the number of genetically labeled β-cells that stained negative for insulin (INS) increased by 2.6-fold compared with wild-type mice (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Part of the YFP+/INS- cells expressed glucagon or somatostatin in adult Akita mice.
source: Part of the YFP+/INS- cells expressed glucagon or somatostatin (0.3% of YFP+/INS- cells; 9 out of 3233 cells) in Akita compared to 0.04% in controls; 3 out of 8091 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data.

claim: The percentage of β-cells expressing PDX-1 and NKX6.1 was decreased in adult Akita mice.
source: The percentage of β-cells expressing transcription factors required for β-cell maturation and function, including PDX-1 and NKX6.1, was decreased in Akita mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some degree of β-cell dedifferentiation/reprogramming takes place in diabetic adult Akita mice.
source: These findings suggest that some degree of β-cell dedifferentiation/reprogramming does take place in diabetic Akita mice; nevertheless, 98.7% of genetically labeled Akita β-cells remained insulin positive (Figure 1d); therefore, these alterations could not explain the 70% decrease in β-cell mass.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's data.

claim: 98.7% of genetically labeled adult Akita β-cells remained insulin positive.
source: These findings suggest that some degree of β-cell dedifferentiation/reprogramming does take place in diabetic Akita mice; nevertheless, 98.7% of genetically labeled Akita β-cells remained insulin positive (Figure 1d); therefore, these alterations could not explain the 70% decrease in β-cell mass.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: β-cell dedifferentiation/reprogramming could not explain the 70% decrease in β-cell mass in adult Akita mice.
source: These findings suggest that some degree of β-cell dedifferentiation/reprogramming does take place in diabetic Akita mice; nevertheless, 98.7% of genetically labeled Akita β-cells remained insulin positive (Figure 1d); therefore, these alterations could not explain the 70% decrease in β-cell mass.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's data.

claim: Decreased β-cell mass in diabetic adult Akita mice is not due to alterations in β-cell proliferation, survival or differentiation in adulthood.
source: Collectively, decreased β-cell mass in diabetic Akita mice is not due to alterations in β-cell proliferation, survival or differentiation in adulthood.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data.

claim: Akita newborns at P1-2 have normal body and pancreatic weight.
source: At this stage, Akita mice have normal body and pancreatic weight (Figure 2a–b) and are strictly normoglycemic (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a–b.

claim: Akita newborns at P1-2 are strictly normoglycemic.
source: At this stage, Akita mice have normal body and pancreatic weight (Figure 2a–b) and are strictly normoglycemic (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: β-Cell mass in Akita newborns at P1-2 was similar to that in control mice.
source: β-Cell mass in Akita newborns was similar to that in control mice (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: β-cell proliferation in Akita newborns at P1-2 was approximately 8-fold higher than in adult animals and was similar to control mice.
source: Furthermore, β-cell proliferation was approximately 8-fold higher than in adult animals and was similar in Akita and control mice (Figure 2e); TUNEL+ β-cells were found neither in control nor in Akita mice (n = 2592 control and 1754 Akita β-cells were counted).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: TUNEL+ β-cells were found neither in control nor in Akita newborns at P1-2.
source: Furthermore, β-cell proliferation was approximately 8-fold higher than in adult animals and was similar in Akita and control mice (Figure 2e); TUNEL+ β-cells were found neither in control nor in Akita mice (n = 2592 control and 1754 Akita β-cells were counted).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data.

claim: In Akita newborns at P1-2, the percentage of NKX6.1 expressing β-cells was similar to that in control mice.
source: In Akita mice, the percentage of NKX6.1 expressing β-cells was similar to that in control mice, whereas there was a small decrease in the percentage of PDX-1 expressing β-cells (Figure 2f–g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2f–g.

claim: In Akita newborns at P1-2, there was a small decrease in the percentage of PDX-1 expressing β-cells.
source: In Akita mice, the percentage of NKX6.1 expressing β-cells was similar to that in control mice, whereas there was a small decrease in the percentage of PDX-1 expressing β-cells (Figure 2f–g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2f–g.

claim: In utero β-cell development in Akita mice is only minimally impaired.
source: Altogether, these findings indicate that in uteroβ-cell development in Akita mice is only minimally impaired, and that β-cell loss must occur after birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data.

claim: β-cell loss in Akita mice must occur after birth.
source: Altogether, these findings indicate that in uteroβ-cell development in Akita mice is only minimally impaired, and that β-cell loss must occur after birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data.

claim: At P19-21, body weight and fed and fasting blood glucose in Akita mice were normal.
source: At this stage, body weight and fed and fasting blood glucose in Akita mice were still normal (Figures 2a and 3a–b); however, the mice exhibited marked β-cell dysfunction, evident by glucose intolerance associated with blunt insulin response to glucose and decreased pancreatic insulin content (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2a and 3a–b.

claim: At P19-21, Akita mice exhibited marked β-cell dysfunction, evident by glucose intolerance associated with blunt insulin response to glucose and decreased pancreatic insulin content.
source: At this stage, body weight and fed and fasting blood glucose in Akita mice were still normal (Figures 2a and 3a–b); however, the mice exhibited marked β-cell dysfunction, evident by glucose intolerance associated with blunt insulin response to glucose and decreased pancreatic insulin content (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3b–d.

claim: Islets isolated from pre-diabetic Akita mice at P19-21 showed marked attenuation of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion along with reduced insulin content.
source: Islets isolated from pre-diabetic Akita mice also showed marked attenuation of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion along with reduced insulin content (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: β-Cell mass was decreased by 60% at P19-21 in Akita mice compared to controls.
source: β-Cell mass was decreased by 60% compared to controls, which is similar to the relative decrease in β-cell mass in adult mice (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The relative decrease in β-cell mass at P19-21 is similar to the relative decrease in β-cell mass in adult Akita mice.
source: β-Cell mass was decreased by 60% compared to controls, which is similar to the relative decrease in β-cell mass in adult mice (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a comparison of data from different time points.

claim: The decrease in β-cell mass at P19-21 was accompanied by a parallel decrease in β-cell proliferation based on Ki67, PCNA and phospho-Histone-H3 immunostaining.
source: This was accompanied by a parallel decrease in β-cell proliferation based on Ki67, PCNA and phospho-Histone-H3 immunostaining (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: In control mice, β-cell proliferation remained high in the first 3 weeks of life.
source: In control mice, β-cell proliferation remained high in the first 3 weeks of life; this was accompanied by two-fold increase in β-cell mass (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4d–e.

claim: In control mice, high β-cell proliferation in the first 3 weeks of life was accompanied by two-fold increase in β-cell mass.
source: In control mice, β-cell proliferation remained high in the first 3 weeks of life; this was accompanied by two-fold increase in β-cell mass (Figure 4d–e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4d–e.

claim: The decline in β-cell proliferation in Akita mice completely prevented the expected early increase of β-cell mass.
source: The decline in β-cell proliferation in Akita mice completely prevented the expected early increase of β-cell mass (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The proliferation rate in the exocrine tissue was similar in wild type mice and in Akita mice at P19-21.
source: The proliferation rate in the exocrine tissue was similar in wild type mice and in Akita mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), indicating that the effect of the Akita mutation on proliferation is cell autonomous.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The effect of the Akita mutation on proliferation is cell autonomous.
source: The proliferation rate in the exocrine tissue was similar in wild type mice and in Akita mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), indicating that the effect of the Akita mutation on proliferation is cell autonomous.
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The weight of the pancreas was similar in Akita and control mice at P19-21.
source: Consistently, the weight of the pancreas, which mainly contains exocrine tissue, was similar in Akita and control mice (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: In control mice, β-cell size remained unchanged during the first 3 weeks of life and increased 3-fold in adult animals.
source: In control mice, β-cell size remained unchanged during the first 3 weeks of life and increased 3-fold in adult animals.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data.

claim: In Akita mice, β-cell size decreased during the early postnatal period, but increased after weaning while developing diabetes.
source: In Akita mice, β-cell size decreased during the early postnatal period, but increased after weaning while developing diabetes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data.

claim: Akita β-cells were smaller than control at P1-2, P19-21 and in 2- to 3-month old animals.
source: Akita β-cells were smaller than control at P1-2, P19-21 and in 2- to 3-month old animals: a 33% reduction in β-cell size was observed in adult Akita mice (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4b–c.

claim: A 33% reduction in β-cell size was observed in adult Akita mice.
source: Akita β-cells were smaller than control at P1-2, P19-21 and in 2- to 3-month old animals: a 33% reduction in β-cell size was observed in adult Akita mice (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4b–c.

claim: β-cell mass increased after weaning both in wild type and in Akita mice.
source: Notably, β-cell mass increased after weaning both in wild type and in Akita mice (Figure 4e); however, the overall increase in β-cell mass in Akita mice was attenuated compared to controls due to the lower rate of β-cell proliferation and smaller increase in β-cell size.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The overall increase in β-cell mass in Akita mice after weaning was attenuated compared to controls due to the lower rate of β-cell proliferation and smaller increase in β-cell size.
source: Notably, β-cell mass increased after weaning both in wild type and in Akita mice (Figure 4e); however, the overall increase in β-cell mass in Akita mice was attenuated compared to controls due to the lower rate of β-cell proliferation and smaller increase in β-cell size.
evidence: This is an interpretation of data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: No TUNEL+ β-cells were detected at P19-21, neither in control nor in Akita mice.
source: We did not detect any TUNEL+ β-cells at P19-21, neither in control nor in Akita mice (n = 2676 control and 1447 Akita β-cells were counted), indicating that apoptotic events were quite rare even in Akita mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data.

claim: Apoptotic events were quite rare in Akita mice at P19-21.
source: We did not detect any TUNEL+ β-cells at P19-21, neither in control nor in Akita mice (n = 2676 control and 1447 Akita β-cells were counted), indicating that apoptotic events were quite rare even in Akita mice.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's data.

claim: Akita β-cell mass is decreased due to impaired postnatal β-cell growth early in life, prior to the onset of full-blown diabetes.
source: In summary, Akita β-cell mass is decreased due to impaired postnatal β-cell growth early in life, prior to the onset of full-blown diabetes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's data.

claim: ER-stress-related genes were upregulated in Akita islets at P19-21.
source: ER-stress-related genes were upregulated in Akita islets, along with modest enrichment of genes involved in apoptosis (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There was modest enrichment of genes involved in apoptosis in Akita islets at P19-21.
source: ER-stress-related genes were upregulated in Akita islets, along with modest enrichment of genes involved in apoptosis (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Total steady state mRNA levels of Xbp1 were decreased in Akita islets at P19-21 with only a modest increase in Xbp1 splicing.
source: Intriguingly, total steady state mRNA levels of Xbp1, the main ER stress-sensing transcription factor, were decreased with only a modest increase in Xbp1 splicing (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The most prominent upregulated UPR gene in Akita islets at P19-21 was Herpud1.
source: The most prominent upregulated UPR gene was Homocysteine-responsive endoplasmic reticulum-resident ubiquitin-like domain member one protein (Herpud1) (log 2FC 1.8; p=4.6×10−24).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: HERPUD1 functions as a hub for membrane association of ER associated degradation (ERAD) machinery components and for the interactions between misfolded proteins and ERAD.
source: HERPUD1 functions as a hub for membrane association of ER associated degradation (ERAD) machinery components and for the interactions between misfolded proteins and ERAD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HERPUD1 function.

claim: The expression of chaperones, including Dnajc3 (Hsp40), Manf and Hspa5 (Bip) was upregulated in Akita islets at P19-21.
source: The expression of chaperones, including Dnajc3 (Hsp40), Manf and Hspa5 (Bip) was upregulated in Akita islets (Figure 5b); the protein level of the latter was also markedly increased (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5b and Western blot data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The protein level of BiP was markedly increased in Akita islets at P19-21.
source: The expression of chaperones, including Dnajc3 (Hsp40), Manf and Hspa5 (Bip) was upregulated in Akita islets (Figure 5b); the protein level of the latter was also markedly increased (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: There was a mixed response of genes that regulate apoptosis in ER stress in Akita islets at P19-21.
source: There was a mixed response of genes that regulate apoptosis in ER stress: Atf6, Atf3, Ddit3 (Chop), Txnip and Bbc3 (Puma) were upregulated, whereas Atf4 and pro-apoptotic Bax were downregulated (the changes in Atf3, Atf4, Atf6 and Bax were not statistically significant) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Atf6, Atf3, Ddit3 (Chop), Txnip and Bbc3 (Puma) were upregulated in Akita islets at P19-21.
source: There was a mixed response of genes that regulate apoptosis in ER stress: Atf6, Atf3, Ddit3 (Chop), Txnip and Bbc3 (Puma) were upregulated, whereas Atf4 and pro-apoptotic Bax were downregulated (the changes in Atf3, Atf4, Atf6 and Bax were not statistically significant) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Atf4 and pro-apoptotic Bax were downregulated in Akita islets at P19-21.
source: There was a mixed response of genes that regulate apoptosis in ER stress: Atf6, Atf3, Ddit3 (Chop), Txnip and Bbc3 (Puma) were upregulated, whereas Atf4 and pro-apoptotic Bax were downregulated (the changes in Atf3, Atf4, Atf6 and Bax were not statistically significant) (Figure 5b).
